newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Mideast envoy made headway on security, not trust.
newsitem.headline: Mideast envoy made headway on security, not trust.

text.p: U.S. envoy Dennis Ross appears to have made some headway in restoring security coordination between Israelis and Palestinians during his mission to the region after last month's Jerusalem suicide bombing.

But by their own assessment, U.S. officials say the seasoned Middle East troubleshooter got hardly anywhere during his four-day shuttle on breaking an icepack of suspicion between the two sides that stands as the biggest obstacle to a peace deal.

One senior American official described Ross's achievements on the core issue of trust on Thursday as "just baby steps" towards changing the adversial mindset that exists between Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat.
"It's easy to break trust. It's very difficult to rebuild it," the official said.
"What we've seen on both sides is a willingness to try and we're going to do our best to encourage that process. That said, it's going to be very difficult."

Ross managed during his trip to establish a trilateral framework for security coordination involving the parties and the United States following the July 30 bombing, which killed 16 people including the two suicide bombers.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright says she will be coming to the Middle East "in the coming days or weeks" as long as she sees results on security and a "100 percent effort" from Arafat to crack down on Islamic militants.

If she comes, she will bring proposals intended to put Israel and the Palestinians on a fast track to a final peace deal at the same time as getting them to fulfil obligations outstanding from their interim agreements since 1993.

When she comes, she has indicated that she will also seek a measure of acceptance from Prime Minister Netanyahu that just as security is Israel's supreme concern, so too some of the actions his right-wing government has taken have contributed to the deadlock in the peace process.

In a keynote speech on her vision of the way forward, Albright referred last week to Israel's building of Jewish settlements on occupied Arab land as one of the policies that Palestinians saw as pre-empting a negotiated peace.
"Let me be clear. There is no moral equivalency between suicide bombers and bulldozers, between killing innocent people and building houses," Albright said.

"It is simply not possible to address political issues seriously in a climate of intimidation and terror. But the principle of refraining from unhelpful unilateral acts is central to maintaining mutual confidence," she said.

Substantive peace talks between Israel and the PLO have been on hold since Israel broke ground in March on a new settlement on the edge of Arab East Jerusalem, which Arafat sees as the capital of a future Palestinian state.
Israel regards all of Jerusalem as its united capital.

Netanyahu, speaking on Wednesday after talks with King Hussein of Jordan on the crisis in the peace process, said he was ready to discuss the issue of settlements in negotiations on a final peace deal.
His government has insisted, however, that it will not contemplate a freeze on the Jerusalem project of Har Homa, a hill Palestinians know as Jabal Abu Ghneim.

Palestinian anger at the scheme has now been compounded by the economic and security siege Netanyahu has slapped on Palestinian areas after last month's attack, a move Arafat sees as a further obstacle to a final peace.
"How can you dance the tango alone? You need a partner who is ready to dance with you," Arafat said in a speech in Ramallah on the West Bank on Thursday.
"We say, 'Is this government really ready to work with us to preserve the peace process and protect it? Is it really ready to do so?' I am sorry to say the answer is no," he said.

Similar language sounds from Israel, where the Jerusalem bombing, its perpetrators as yet unidentified, appears to have convinced Netanyahu that Arafat has loosened the screws on Moslem militants to pressure the Jewish state into concessions.

A senior aide to Netanyahu, David Bar-Illan, said Israel was still waiting to see whether the Ross security framework would prove more than just meetings. "The success will be measured by the results and the results are not in," he said.
In the midst of the mutual recrimination, Albright must now assess whether the time is right for her first trip to the region since taking office six months ago.
As she weighs her decision, U.S. officials are urging both parties not only to cooperate on security but also to lower the noise level.

"We think it's very important that as difficult as it is, both sides need to tone down the rhetoric. And I mean both sides," the senior American official said. "It may make good television but it doesn't help the process."
